<problem>
Let \(\mathbb N=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}\), and let \(m,n\) be positive integers with \(\gcd(m,n)=1\). Set
\[
d=m^2+n(2m+1),\qquad (a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)=\bigl(0,nm,n(m+1),n(2m+1),d\bigr),
\]
and let \(A=\{a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4\}\).

For each integer \(h\ge0\), let \(hA\) be the set of sums of exactly \(h\) elements of \(A\), with repetitions allowed and \(0A=\{0\}\). Define the additive semigroups
\[
S_1=\left\{\sum_{i=0}^4u_i a_i:u_i\in\mathbb N\right\},\qquad
S_2=\left\{\sum_{i=0}^4u_i(d-a_i):u_i\in\mathbb N\right\}.
\]
For \(j=1,2\), let their conductors be
\[
c_j=\min\{c\in\mathbb N:c+\mathbb N\subseteq S_j\}.
\]
Define the sumsets regularity \(\sigma(A)\) to be the least \(h_0\in\mathbb N\) such that, for every integer \(h\ge h_0\), both \(hd\ge c_1+c_2\) and
\[
hA=\{x\in\mathbb Z:0\le x\le hd,\ x\in S_1,\ hd-x\in S_2\}
\]
hold. The inequality \(hd\ge c_1+c_2\) is part of this definition, even when the displayed set equality holds at earlier levels.

Let \(P=\mathbb C[x_0,x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4]\), with \(\deg x_i=1\), and let \(\varphi:P\to\mathbb C[s,t]\) be the algebra homomorphism \(x_i\mapsto s^{a_i}t^{d-a_i}\), where \(s,t\) are independent variables. Give \(R_A=P/\ker\varphi\) its quotient grading. If its minimal graded free \(P\)-resolution has modules
\[
F_i=\bigoplus_jP(-j)^{\beta_{i,j}},
\]
where the generator of \(P(-j)\) has degree \(j\), define
\[
\operatorname{reg}(A)=\max\{j-i:\beta_{i,j}\ne0\}.
\]
Thus this is the regularity of the coordinate ring, not its defining ideal.

Determine the exact function \(\Delta(m,n)=\sigma(A)-\operatorname{reg}(A)\) for every coprime positive pair \((m,n)\).
</problem>

28	## 1. A free module basis
29	
30	Write \(R=R_A\), and use \(x_i\) also for its image in \(R\). Thus
31	\[
32	x_0=t^d,\qquad x_4=s^d,
33	\]
34	so
35	\[
36	B=\mathbb C[x_0,x_4]\subseteq R
37	\]
38	is a polynomial ring in two degree-one variables.
39	
40	Set
41	\[
42	M=m+n-1.
43	\]
44	For \(u,v\in\mathbb N\), define
45	\[
46	b_{u,v}
47	=x_1^{\max(u-v,0)}
48	 x_2^{\max(v-u,0)}
49	 x_3^{\min(u,v)}.
50	\]
51	Its degree and its exponent of \(s\) are, respectively,
52	\[
53	e(u,v)=\max(u,v),\qquad
54	\alpha(u,v)=n\bigl(mu+(m+1)v\bigr).
55	\]
56	Its exponent of \(t\) is therefore
57	\[
58	\beta(u,v)=e(u,v)d-\alpha(u,v).
59	\]

61	Consider the finite set
62	\[
63	D=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb N^2: u,v\le M,\ |u-v|\le m\}.
64	\]
65	
66	### Lemma
67	The elements \(b_{u,v}\), for \((u,v)\in D\), form a free \(B\)-basis of \(R\).
68	
69	### Proof: spanning
70	
71	Since \(a_1+a_2=a_3\), we have
72	\[
73	x_1x_2=x_0x_3.
74	\]
75	Consequently, every monomial in \(x_1,x_2,x_3\) is an \(x_0\)-multiple of some \(b_{u,v}\). It suffices to reduce arbitrary pairs \((u,v)\) to \(D\).
76	
77	For this purpose put
78	\[
79	k(u,v)=mu+(m+1)v,\qquad H=\max(u,v).
80	\]
81	Two monomials in \(R\) are equal whenever they have the same degree and the same \(s\)-exponent.
82	
83	First reduce the imbalance.
84	
85	* If \(u-v>m\), replace
86	  \[
87	  (u,v)\longmapsto(u-m-1,v+m).
88	  \]
89	* If \(v-u>m\), replace
90	  \[
91	  (u,v)\longmapsto(u+m+1,v-m).
92	  \]
93	
94	Both operations preserve \(k(u,v)\), keep the coordinates nonnegative, do not increase \(H\), and strictly decrease \(|u-v|\). If the new maximum is \(H'\), they give the identity
95	\[
96	b_{u,v}=x_0^{H-H'}b_{u',v'}.
97	\]
98	
99	Once \(|u-v|\le m\), suppose \(H\ge m+n\).
100	
101	* If \(u\ge v\), replace
102	  \[
103	  (u,v)\longmapsto(u-m-n,v-n).
104	  \]
105	  Both new coordinates are nonnegative because \(v\ge u-m\ge n\).
106	* If \(v>u\), replace
107	  \[
108	  (u,v)\longmapsto(u-n+1,v-m-n).
109	  \]
110	  Again both new coordinates are nonnegative, because \(u\ge v-m\ge n\).
111	
112	In either case,
113	\[
114	k(u,v)-k(u',v')=d,
115	\qquad H'\le H-n.
116	\]
117	Thus
118	\[
119	b_{u,v}=x_0^{H-H'-n}x_4^n b_{u',v'}.
120	\]
121	The exponent of \(x_0\) is nonnegative.
122	
123	Repeating these operations terminates: an imbalance operation decreases the lexicographic pair \((H,|u-v|)\), and an endpoint operation decreases \(H\). At termination the pair lies in \(D\). This proves spanning over \(B\).
124	
125	### Proof: independence
126	
127	Counting by the value of \(u-v\),
128	\[
129	\begin{aligned}
130	|D|
131	&=(M+1)+2\sum_{i=1}^{m}(M-i+1)\\
132	&=(2m+1)(M+1)-m(m+1)\\
133	&=m^2+(2m+1)n=d.
134	\end{aligned}
135	\]
136	
137	Moreover,
138	\[
139	\gcd(nm,n(m+1),d)=1,
140	\]
141	because \(\gcd(n,d)=\gcd(n,m^2)=1\). Hence nonnegative combinations of \(nm\) and \(n(m+1)\) attain every residue modulo \(d\). The reductions above preserve the \(s\)-exponent modulo \(d\), so the \(d\) elements indexed by \(D\) attain all \(d\) residues. They therefore attain each residue exactly once.
142	
143	Different basis candidates consequently have disjoint \(s\)-exponent residues modulo \(d\), whereas multiplication by \(B\) preserves those residues. Within one candidate, multiplication by the polynomial ring \(\mathbb C[s^d,t^d]\) is injective. Thus the spanning sum is direct:
144	\[
145	\boxed{\displaystyle
146	R=\bigoplus_{(u,v)\in D}B\,b_{u,v}.}
147	\]
148	This proves the lemma. \(\square\)

150	## 2. The regularity
151	
152	The free decomposition shows that \(x_0,x_4\) is an \(R\)-regular sequence. It also shows that
153	\[
154	E=R/(x_0,x_4)R
155	\]
156	has vector-space basis given by the images of the \(b_{u,v}\), \((u,v)\in D\). Its highest nonzero degree is
157	\[
158	M,
159	\]
160	since all basis degrees are at most \(M\), and \((M,M)\in D\).
161	
162	For completeness, this determines the regularity in exactly the convention of the question.
163	
164	Tensoring the minimal graded \(P\)-resolution of \(R\) with
165	\[
166	Q=P/(x_0,x_4)=\mathbb C[x_1,x_2,x_3]
167	\]
168	preserves exactness because \(x_0,x_4\) is \(R\)-regular. The resulting resolution is minimal and has the same graded shifts. Thus
169	\[
170	\operatorname{reg}_P(R)=\operatorname{reg}_Q(E).
171	\]
172	
173	The Koszul complex of \(E\) over \(Q\) gives
174	\[
175	\operatorname{Tor}_i^Q(E,\mathbb C)_j=0
176	\quad\text{if }j>M+i.
177	\]
178	On the other hand, any nonzero element of \(E_M\) is annihilated by all three variables. It gives a nonzero top Koszul-homology class in degree \(M+3\). Hence
179	\[
180	\operatorname{reg}_Q(E)=M.
181	\]
182	Therefore
183	\[
184	\boxed{\operatorname{reg}(A)=m+n-1.}
185	\]
186	
187	## 3. The sumset equality holds at every level
188	
189	Index the basis elements by their \(s\)-exponent residues \(r\pmod d\), writing their data as
190	\[
191	(\alpha_r,\beta_r,e_r),\qquad
192	\alpha_r+\beta_r=e_rd.
193	\]
194	
195	The free-basis decomposition implies that the exponent pairs occurring in \(R\), in residue \(r\), are exactly
196	\[
197	(\alpha_r+qd,\ \beta_r+pd),
198	\qquad p,q\in\mathbb N.
199	\]
200	
201	In particular:
202	
203	* \(\alpha_r\) is the least element of \(S_1\) congruent to \(r\pmod d\);
204	* \(\beta_r\) is the least element of \(S_2\) congruent to \(-r\pmod d\).
205	
206	Now suppose
207	\[
208	0\le x\le hd,\qquad x\in S_1,\qquad hd-x\in S_2.
209	\]
210	Choose \(r\equiv x\pmod d\). Then
211	\[
212	x=\alpha_r+qd,\qquad
213	hd-x=\beta_r+pd
214	\]
215	for some \(p,q\in\mathbb N\). Adding gives
216	\[
217	h=e_r+p+q.
218	\]
219	Thus \(x_4^qx_0^pb_r\) is a degree-\(h\) monomial with \(s\)-exponent \(x\), proving \(x\in hA\).
220	
221	The converse follows immediately from the definitions. Hence, for **every** \(h\ge0\),
222	\[
223	\boxed{\displaystyle
224	hA=\{x:0\le x\le hd,\ x\in S_1,\ hd-x\in S_2\}.}
225	\]
226	
227	The conductor inequality in the question is therefore the only restriction on \(\sigma(A)\):
228	\[
229	\boxed{\displaystyle
230	\sigma(A)=\left\lceil\frac{c_1+c_2}{d}\right\rceil .}
231	\]
232	
233	## 4. Computing the conductors
234	
235	If a numerical semigroup contains \(d\), and its least elements in the \(d\) residue classes are \(w_r\), its conductor is
236	\[
237	c=\max_r w_r-d+1.
238	\]
239	Indeed, the largest missing integer in residue \(r\), when nonnegative, is \(w_r-d\). This formula also gives \(c=0\) for \(\mathbb N\).
240	
241	Our basis supplies precisely these least elements.
242	
243	### The first conductor
244	
245	Since \(u,v\le M\),
246	\[
247	\max_D\alpha(u,v)=n(2m+1)M,
248	\]
249	attained at \(u=v=M\). Thus
250	\[
251	\boxed{\displaystyle c_1=n(2m+1)M-d+1.}
252	\]
253	
254	### The second conductor
255	
256	If \(u\ge v\), then
257	\[
258	\beta(u,v)=m^2u+n(m+1)(u-v)
259	\le m^2M+nm(m+1).
260	\]
261	Equality holds at
262	\[
263	(u,v)=(M,M-m)=(M,n-1).
264	\]
265	
266	If \(v\ge u\), then
267	\[
268	\beta(u,v)=m^2v+nm(v-u)
269	\le m^2M+nm^2,
270	\]
271	which is no larger. Consequently,
272	\[
273	\max_D\beta(u,v)
274	=m^2M+nm(m+1)
275	=m(d-m).
276	\]
277	Therefore
278	\[
279	\boxed{\displaystyle
280	c_2=m(d-m)-d+1=(m-1)(d-m-1).}
281	\]
282	
283	It follows that
284	\[
285	c_1+c_2
286	=n(2m+1)M+(m-2)d-m^2+2.
287	\]
288	Since \(M\) is an integer,
289	\[
290	\Delta
291	=\left\lceil\frac{c_1+c_2-Md}{d}\right\rceil.
292	\]
293	Finally,
294	\[
295	c_1+c_2-Md
296	=(n-2)m^2-(3m+2)n+2,
297	\]
298	which proves the claimed formula.
299	
300	## 5. Executable verification
301	
302	The following is pure Python. It does more than evaluate the formulas:
303	
304	1. It checks the reduction identities and basis residues.
305	2. It independently computes both Apéry sets by shortest paths.
306	3. It constructs actual sumsets and checks the equality at every tested level.
307	4. It checks the Hilbert function against the free-basis decomposition.
308	5. It computes graded Betti numbers directly from the five-generator Koszul complex, using exact rational ranks.
309	
310	For the Betti checks, degrees through \(M+5\) cover every possible nonzero Betti number by the regularity bound proved above and the length-five Koszul complex.

26	## 1. A free module basis
27	
28	Write \(R=R_A\), and use \(x_i\) also for its image in \(R\). Thus
29	\[
30	x_0=t^d,\qquad x_4=s^d,
31	\]
32	so
33	\[
34	B=\mathbb C[x_0,x_4]\subseteq R
35	\]
36	is a polynomial ring in two degree-one variables.
37	
38	Set
39	\[
40	M=m+n-1.
41	\]
42	For \(u,v\in\mathbb N\), define
43	\[
44	b_{u,v}
45	=x_1^{\max(u-v,0)}
46	 x_2^{\max(v-u,0)}
47	 x_3^{\min(u,v)}.
48	\]
49	Its degree and its exponent of \(s\) are, respectively,
50	\[
51	e(u,v)=\max(u,v),\qquad
52	\alpha(u,v)=n\bigl(mu+(m+1)v\bigr).
53	\]
54	Its exponent of \(t\) is therefore
55	\[
56	\beta(u,v)=e(u,v)d-\alpha(u,v).
57	\]
58	
59	Consider the finite set
60	\[
61	D=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb N^2: u,v\le M,\ |u-v|\le m\}.
62	\]
63	
64	### Lemma
65	The elements \(b_{u,v}\), for \((u,v)\in D\), form a free \(B\)-basis of \(R\).
66	
67	### Proof: spanning
68	
69	Since \(a_1+a_2=a_3\), we have
70	\[
71	x_1x_2=x_0x_3.
72	\]
73	Consequently, every monomial in \(x_1,x_2,x_3\) is an \(x_0\)-multiple of some \(b_{u,v}\). It suffices to reduce arbitrary pairs \((u,v)\) to \(D\).
74	
75	For this purpose put
76	\[
77	k(u,v)=mu+(m+1)v,\qquad H=\max(u,v).
78	\]
79	Two monomials in \(R\) are equal whenever they have the same degree and the same \(s\)-exponent.
80	
81	First reduce the imbalance.
82	
83	* If \(u-v>m\), replace
84	  \[
85	  (u,v)\longmapsto(u-m-1,v+m).
86	  \]
87	* If \(v-u>m\), replace
88	  \[
89	  (u,v)\longmapsto(u+m+1,v-m).
90	  \]
91	
92	Both operations preserve \(k(u,v)\), keep the coordinates nonnegative, do not increase \(H\), and strictly decrease \(|u-v|\). If the new maximum is \(H'\), they give the identity
93	\[
94	b_{u,v}=x_0^{H-H'}b_{u',v'}.
95	\]
96	
97	Once \(|u-v|\le m\), suppose \(H\ge m+n\).
98	
99	* If \(u\ge v\), replace
100	  \[
101	  (u,v)\longmapsto(u-m-n,v-n).
102	  \]
103	  Both new coordinates are nonnegative because \(v\ge u-m\ge n\).
104	* If \(v>u\), replace
105	  \[
106	  (u,v)\longmapsto(u-n+1,v-m-n).
107	  \]
108	  Again both new coordinates are nonnegative, because \(u\ge v-m\ge n\).
109	
110	In either case,
111	\[
112	k(u,v)-k(u',v')=d,
113	\qquad H'\le H-n.
114	\]
115	Thus
116	\[
117	b_{u,v}=x_0^{H-H'-n}x_4^n b_{u',v'}.
118	\]
119	The exponent of \(x_0\) is nonnegative.
120	
121	Repeating these operations terminates: an imbalance operation decreases the lexicographic pair \((H,|u-v|)\), and an endpoint operation decreases \(H\). At termination the pair lies in \(D\). This proves spanning over \(B\).
122	
123	### Proof: independence
124	
125	Counting by the value of \(u-v\),
126	\[
127	\begin{aligned}
128	|D|
129	&=(M+1)+2\sum_{i=1}^{m}(M-i+1)\\
130	&=(2m+1)(M+1)-m(m+1)\\
131	&=m^2+(2m+1)n=d.
132	\end{aligned}
133	\]
134	
135	Moreover,
136	\[
137	\gcd(nm,n(m+1),d)=1,
138	\]
139	because \(\gcd(n,d)=\gcd(n,m^2)=1\). Hence nonnegative combinations of \(nm\) and \(n(m+1)\) attain every residue modulo \(d\). The reductions above preserve the \(s\)-exponent modulo \(d\), so the \(d\) elements indexed by \(D\) attain all \(d\) residues. They therefore attain each residue exactly once.
140	
141	Different basis candidates consequently have disjoint \(s\)-exponent residues modulo \(d\), whereas multiplication by \(B\) preserves those residues. Within one candidate, multiplication by the polynomial ring \(\mathbb C[s^d,t^d]\) is injective. Thus the spanning sum is direct:
142	\[
143	\boxed{\displaystyle
144	R=\bigoplus_{(u,v)\in D}B\,b_{u,v}.}
145	\]
146	This proves the lemma. \(\square\)

148	## 2. The regularity
149	
150	The free decomposition shows that \(x_0,x_4\) is an \(R\)-regular sequence. It also shows that
151	\[
152	E=R/(x_0,x_4)R
153	\]
154	has vector-space basis given by the images of the \(b_{u,v}\), \((u,v)\in D\). Its highest nonzero degree is
155	\[
156	M,
157	\]
158	since all basis degrees are at most \(M\), and \((M,M)\in D\).
159	
160	For completeness, this determines the regularity in exactly the convention of the question.
161	
162	Tensoring the minimal graded \(P\)-resolution of \(R\) with
163	\[
164	Q=P/(x_0,x_4)=\mathbb C[x_1,x_2,x_3]
165	\]
166	preserves exactness because \(x_0,x_4\) is \(R\)-regular. The resulting resolution is minimal and has the same graded shifts. Thus
167	\[
168	\operatorname{reg}_P(R)=\operatorname{reg}_Q(E).
169	\]
170	
171	The Koszul complex of \(E\) over \(Q\) gives
172	\[
173	\operatorname{Tor}_i^Q(E,\mathbb C)_j=0
174	\quad\text{if }j>M+i.
175	\]
176	On the other hand, any nonzero element of \(E_M\) is annihilated by all three variables. It gives a nonzero top Koszul-homology class in degree \(M+3\). Hence
177	\[
178	\operatorname{reg}_Q(E)=M.
179	\]
180	Therefore
181	\[
182	\boxed{\operatorname{reg}(A)=m+n-1.}
183	\]

185	## 3. The sumset equality holds at every level
186	
187	Index the basis elements by their \(s\)-exponent residues \(r\pmod d\), writing their data as
188	\[
189	(\alpha_r,\beta_r,e_r),\qquad
190	\alpha_r+\beta_r=e_rd.
191	\]
192	
193	The free-basis decomposition implies that the exponent pairs occurring in \(R\), in residue \(r\), are exactly
194	\[
195	(\alpha_r+qd,\ \beta_r+pd),
196	\qquad p,q\in\mathbb N.
197	\]
198	
199	In particular:
200	
201	* \(\alpha_r\) is the least element of \(S_1\) congruent to \(r\pmod d\);
202	* \(\beta_r\) is the least element of \(S_2\) congruent to \(-r\pmod d\).
203	
204	Now suppose
205	\[
206	0\le x\le hd,\qquad x\in S_1,\qquad hd-x\in S_2.
207	\]
208	Choose \(r\equiv x\pmod d\). Then
209	\[
210	x=\alpha_r+qd,\qquad
211	hd-x=\beta_r+pd
212	\]
213	for some \(p,q\in\mathbb N\). Adding gives
214	\[
215	h=e_r+p+q.
216	\]
217	Thus \(x_4^qx_0^pb_r\) is a degree-\(h\) monomial with \(s\)-exponent \(x\), proving \(x\in hA\).
218	
219	The converse follows immediately from the definitions. Hence, for **every** \(h\ge0\),
220	\[
221	\boxed{\displaystyle
222	hA=\{x:0\le x\le hd,\ x\in S_1,\ hd-x\in S_2\}.}
223	\]
224	
225	The conductor inequality in the question is therefore the only restriction on \(\sigma(A)\):
226	\[
227	\boxed{\displaystyle
228	\sigma(A)=\left\lceil\frac{c_1+c_2}{d}\right\rceil .}
229	\]

231	## 4. Computing the conductors
232	
233	If a numerical semigroup contains \(d\), and its least elements in the \(d\) residue classes are \(w_r\), its conductor is
234	\[
235	c=\max_r w_r-d+1.
236	\]
237	Indeed, the largest missing integer in residue \(r\), when nonnegative, is \(w_r-d\). This formula also gives \(c=0\) for \(\mathbb N\).
238	
239	Our basis supplies precisely these least elements.
240	
241	### The first conductor
242	
243	Since \(u,v\le M\),
244	\[
245	\max_D\alpha(u,v)=n(2m+1)M,
246	\]
247	attained at \(u=v=M\). Thus
248	\[
249	\boxed{\displaystyle c_1=n(2m+1)M-d+1.}
250	\]
251	
252	### The second conductor
253	
254	If \(u\ge v\), then
255	\[
256	\beta(u,v)=m^2u+n(m+1)(u-v)
257	\le m^2M+nm(m+1).
258	\]
259	Equality holds at
260	\[
261	(u,v)=(M,M-m)=(M,n-1).
262	\]
263	
264	If \(v\ge u\), then
265	\[
266	\beta(u,v)=m^2v+nm(v-u)
267	\le m^2M+nm^2,
268	\]
269	which is no larger. Consequently,
270	\[
271	\max_D\beta(u,v)
272	=m^2M+nm(m+1)
273	=m(d-m).
274	\]
275	Therefore
276	\[
277	\boxed{\displaystyle
278	c_2=m(d-m)-d+1=(m-1)(d-m-1).}
279	\]
280	
281	It follows that
282	\[
283	c_1+c_2
284	=n(2m+1)M+(m-2)d-m^2+2.
285	\]
286	Since \(M\) is an integer,
287	\[
288	\Delta
289	=\left\lceil\frac{c_1+c_2-Md}{d}\right\rceil.
290	\]
291	Finally,
292	\[
293	c_1+c_2-Md
294	=(n-2)m^2-(3m+2)n+2,
295	\]
296	which proves the claimed formula.

306	5. It computes graded Betti numbers directly from the five-generator Koszul complex, using exact rational ranks.

358	    dist = [None] * d
359	    dist[0] = 0
